Style Notes

The history behind each Backing Track style, and what to listen to

Every Backing Track style: what it is, a little history, what the band plays and what it leaves out, and recordings to hear it played properly.

Each style in the Backing Track imitates a real band. This page says which one: where the style came from, what the band’s bass, comping and drums are copying (and what they leave out), and the recordings to hear it played properly.

Jazz

Swing

Walking bass, the ride cymbal and syncopated comping

Open the Swing style in the Backing Track

What it is

The rhythm section of small-group jazz from the late 1930s onward: a bass that plays a note on every beat, a drummer whose main voice is the ride cymbal (ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a) with the hi-hat closing on 2 and 4, and a piano or guitar that “comps” (accompanies, complements): short chords placed off the beat, answering the soloist instead of marking time.

A little history

In the 1920s the bass part of a jazz band was usually a tuba or a slapped string bass playing on beats 1 and 3 (the two-beat feel; see Jazz ballad). In the Count Basie band of the mid-1930s, bassist Walter Page walked four even beats a bar, guitarist Freddie Green strummed a quiet chord on every beat, and drummer Jo Jones moved the time-keeping from the bass drum to the hi-hat. Basie himself played sparse fills instead of a full stride left hand. That “All-American Rhythm Section” is where the modern swing feel comes from.

In the 1940s bebop drummers (Kenny Clarke, then Max Roach) moved the pulse to the ride cymbal and used the snare and bass drum for accents (“dropping bombs”). Pianists such as Bud Powell stopped playing on every beat and comped in short syncopated stabs. By the late 1950s, rootless left-hand voicings (Bill Evans, Wynton Kelly, Red Garland) became the standard piano sound: the bassist has the root, so the pianist plays the 3rd, 7th and colour tones. That is the sound the band’s piano uses here.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Walking: root on beat 1, chord tones and scale steps, an approach note on beat 4.
  • Comping: syncopated rhythms chosen from a set of figures (the Charleston, anticipations, and so on).
  • Drums: ride-cymbal pattern, hi-hat on 2 and 4, light comping on the snare.
  • Voicings: rootless piano voicings, shell voicings on guitar. Players add unmarked 9ths and 13ths.

Real walking lines move far more freely than any rule set; the band’s bassist is a beginner’s model.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
Count Basie Orchestra, One O’Clock Jump 1937 Walter Page’s four-to-the-bar bass, Freddie Green’s guitar, Jo Jones on hi-hat.
Count Basie, Lester Leaps In (Kansas City Seven) 1939 The same rhythm section in a small group behind Lester Young.
Miles Davis Quintet, Oleo (Relaxin’) 1956 Paul Chambers walking, Philly Joe Jones on the ride, Red Garland’s comping.
Miles Davis, Freddie Freeloader (Kind of Blue) 1959 A jazz blues; Wynton Kelly’s comping behind the horns.
Oscar Peterson Trio, C Jam Blues (Night Train) 1962 Ray Brown’s walking bass at its most driving.
More recent
Recording Year Listen for
Tony Bennett & Lady Gaga, Anything Goes (Cheek to Cheek) 2014 A small group walking and swinging behind two singers.
Jon Batiste, I Need You (We Are) 2021 Swing-era rhythm in a Grammy-winning pop record.

Sources

  • Gunther Schuller, The Swing Era (Oxford, 1989), on the Basie rhythm section.
  • Paul Berliner, Thinking in Jazz (Chicago, 1994), chapters on the rhythm section and comping.
  • Mark Levine, The Jazz Piano Book (Sher, 1989), on rootless voicings.

Jazz ballad

Bass in two, long chords, quiet time

Open the Jazz ballad style in the Backing Track

What it is

A slow standard played by a jazz rhythm section: the bass on beats 1 and 3 (a two-feel), held chords on the piano, and brushes stirring the snare or a soft ride. The band leaves room for the melody.

A little history

The two-feel is older than walking bass. New Orleans and 1920s dance bands put the tuba or string bass on 1 and 3, and when the bass began walking in the 1930s (see Swing), the two-feel stayed on as the lighter gear: bands play the head of a tune in two and start walking for the solos. On ballads it never has to leave. Brushes, used on drums since the 1920s, became the ballad sound through drummers such as Jo Jones and later Philly Joe Jones and Ed Thigpen. Pianists filled the long chords with the rich voicings that came from Ellington, Billy Strayhorn and later Bill Evans.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Two-feel: root on 1, fifth on 3, now and then a pickup into the next bar.
  • Comping: long held chords (pad).
  • Drums: quiet time. Voicings: rootless, with unmarked extensions.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
Coleman Hawkins, Body and Soul 1939 The tenor ballad everyone learned; the band barely there.
Miles Davis, ’Round Midnight (’Round About Midnight) 1956 Harmon mute over Paul Chambers in two.
Bill Evans Trio, My Foolish Heart (Waltz for Debby) 1961 Paul Motian’s brushes; Scott LaFaro’s bass.
John Coltrane, Ballads 1962 A whole album of the form; McCoy Tyner’s voicings.
John Coltrane & Johnny Hartman, My One and Only Love 1963 Ballad accompaniment behind a singer.
More recent
Recording Year Listen for
Tony Bennett & Amy Winehouse, Body and Soul 2011 The same tune as Hawkins, with a quiet trio under the voices.
Laufey, Valentine (Everything I Know About Love) 2022 A jazz-ballad band under a young pop singer.

Sources

  • Paul Berliner, Thinking in Jazz (Chicago, 1994), on the two-feel and on brushes.
  • Ted Gioia, The Jazz Standards (Oxford, 2012), entries for the tunes above.

Boogaloo

Straight eighths, a bass riff and chord stabs, from soul jazz

Open the Boogaloo style in the Backing Track

What it is

A jazz band playing straight (not swung) eighth notes over a repeated bass figure, with piano or organ chords locked to the riff and a backbeat on the drums. It sits between hard bop, R&B and Latin music.

A little history

The word covers two related things from the mid-1960s. Latin boogaloo was a New York dance music that mixed Cuban son and mambo with R&B; Joe Cuba’s Bang! Bang! (1966) and Pete Rodríguez’s I Like It Like That (1967) were hits. In jazz, soul jazz players on labels like Blue Note took up the same straight eighths. Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man (1962) and Lee Morgan’s The Sidewinder (recorded 1963) came first, and Lou Donaldson’s Alligator Bogaloo (1967) put the name on the jazz version. Drummers such as Idris Muhammad and Bernard Purdie played a backbeat with busy sixteenth-note hi-hats; the tunes were often blues forms over one riff. Mongo Santamaría’s cover of Watermelon Man (1963) carried the Latin side, with congas, back into the charts, which is why the band adds a conga tumbao.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Boogaloo riff: root on 1, root pushed on the and of 2, fifth and flat seventh on 4.
  • Comping: stabs on the same rhythm as the riff.
  • Drums: straight-eighth backbeat. Congas: a tumbao.
  • Voicings: rootless jazz voicings.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
Herbie Hancock, Watermelon Man (Takin’ Off) 1962 The riff in the bass and piano left hand; Billy Higgins’ even eighths.
Mongo Santamaría, Watermelon Man 1963 The same tune with congas and a Latin band.
Lee Morgan, The Sidewinder 1963 rec., 1964 A 24-bar blues on a boogaloo groove; the record that sold Blue Note on the feel.
Joe Cuba Sextet, Bang! Bang! 1966 Latin boogaloo: party noise over a piano montuno.
Lou Donaldson, Alligator Bogaloo 1967 Improvised as filler in the studio; Lonnie Smith’s organ, George Benson’s guitar, Idris Muhammad (then Leo Morris) on drums.
More recent
Recording Year Listen for
Us3, Cantaloop (Flip Fantasia) 1993 Built on Herbie Hancock’s Cantaloupe Island (1964): the soul-jazz riff under hip-hop drums.
Herbie Hancock, Watermelon Man (Head Hunters) 1973 The same tune redone as funk, for comparison.

Sources

  • Blue Note, “Lou Donaldson: the fortuitously funky Alligator Bogaloo”
  • Wikipedia, Alligator Bogaloo: recorded 7 April 1967, Van Gelder Studio.
  • Juan Flores, From Bomba to Hip-Hop (Columbia, 2000), chapter on Latin boogaloo.

Ragtime

A march for the piano, with the melody ragged against it

Open the Ragtime style in the Backing Track

What it is

Composed piano music from about 1895 to 1920, built like a march: several 16-bar strains, a left hand that plays a bass note on the beat and a chord off it, and a right hand whose melody is syncopated (“ragged”) against that steady left hand. Its eighth notes are straight, not swung.

Ragtime is where stride came from: the stride left hand is the ragtime left hand, played faster and swung, with songs and the blues in place of written rags. The lesson Two Left Hands plays the two one after the other.

A little history

Ragtime grew among Black pianists in the saloons and dance halls of the Mississippi valley in the 1890s, and became the first African American music to sell across the country, mostly as sheet music for parlour pianos. Scott Joplin’s Maple Leaf Rag (1899), published in Sedalia, Missouri, sold hundreds of thousands of copies. Joplin, James Scott and Joseph Lamb wrote the “classic rags”; Tin Pan Alley turned out ragtime songs by the thousand. Bands played rags too, and ragtime fed straight into early jazz in New Orleans and into Harlem stride.

It was largely forgotten until the 1970s, when Joshua Rifkin’s recordings of Joplin and the film The Sting (1973), with Marvin Hamlisch’s arrangement of The Entertainer, brought it back.

The band’s version

  • Comping: Stride: on the piano, a low bass note on 1 and 3 and the chord on 2 and 4, in straight time.
  • Bass: Root and fifth on 1 and 3, like the tuba in a march band.
  • Drums: Boom-chick: kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
  • Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

A rag is written down, and its right-hand melody is the point. The band plays only the left hand’s pattern; the ragged melody is yours.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
Scott Joplin, Maple Leaf Rag (piano roll) 1916 Joplin’s own playing, as near as a roll allows.
Jelly Roll Morton, Maple Leaf Rag (Library of Congress) 1938 Morton showing how New Orleans turned the rag into jazz.
Joshua Rifkin, Piano Rags by Scott Joplin 1970 Rags played as written, slowly, as Joplin asked.
Marvin Hamlisch, The Entertainer (The Sting) 1973 The record that brought ragtime back.

Sources

  • Edward A. Berlin, Ragtime: A Musical and Cultural History (California, 1980).
  • Rudi Blesh and Harriet Janis, They All Played Ragtime (Knopf, 1950).
  • Gunther Schuller, Early Jazz (Oxford, 1968).

Stride Piano

A left hand that leaps: bass note, chord, bass note, chord

Open the Stride piano style in the Backing Track

What it is

Solo piano music from Harlem in the late 1910s to the 1930s. The left hand does the work of a whole rhythm section: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4, the hand leaping (“striding”) between them on every beat. The right hand plays the melody, decorated, over it.

Stride and boogie-woogie grew up side by side: both are piano music for dancing at parties, both put a whole band into the left hand, and both feed into swing. They differ in what the left hand does. The lesson Two Left Hands plays them side by side.

A little history

Stride comes out of ragtime. A Scott Joplin rag already has the oom-pah left hand, written as a march. In New York around the First World War, pianists such as James P. Johnson, Luckey Roberts and Willie “The Lion” Smith played it faster and swung it, took it from rags to popular songs and the blues, and added runs, tenths and cross-rhythms. They played at rent parties, where tenants paid the rent by charging for food, drink and music, and in cutting contests against each other. Johnson’s Carolina Shout was the test piece: Duke Ellington learned it from a piano roll, slowed down.

Johnson’s pupil Fats Waller made stride popular on records and radio, from 1934 with a small band, Fats Waller and His Rhythm: bass, drums and guitar playing in two under the piano’s left hand. That is the sound this style copies. Art Tatum took stride to its technical limit; Count Basie began as a stride pianist and pared it down to almost nothing; Thelonious Monk kept stride passages in his playing all his life.

Johnson also wrote Charleston (1923). Its rhythm, a long note on 1 and a short one on the and of 2, is the Charleston comping figure jazz pianists still use.

The band’s version

  • Comping: Stride: on the piano, a low bass note on 1 and 3 (the root as an octave where a chord starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.
  • Bass: Two-feel: half notes on 1 and 3, with the piano’s left hand.
  • Drums: Jazz time, lightly.
  • Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Real stride left hands reach for tenths, walk them up and down between chords, and break the pattern for a run; the right hand carries the tune. The band’s pianist keeps the pattern and plays no melody. That is your part.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
James P. Johnson, Carolina Shout 1921 The test piece of the Harlem pianists.
Fats Waller, Handful of Keys 1929 Stride at speed, solo.
Fats Waller, Ain’t Misbehavin’ (solo piano) 1929 The same left hand under a song.
Fats Waller and His Rhythm, I’m Gonna Sit Right Down and Write Myself a Letter 1935 Stride piano with bass and drums: this style.
Art Tatum, Tiger Rag 1933 Stride as virtuoso display.
Willie “The Lion” Smith, Echoes of Spring 1939 A gentler, more harmonic stride.

Sources

  • Gunther Schuller, Early Jazz (Oxford, 1968), on James P. Johnson and the Harlem pianists.
  • Willie “The Lion” Smith with George Hoefer, Music on My Mind (Doubleday, 1964), on rent parties and cutting contests.
  • Scott E. Brown, James P. Johnson: A Case of Mistaken Identity (Scarecrow, 1986).
  • Riccardo Scivales, Jazz Piano: The Left Hand (Ekay, 1990), on stride and boogie-woogie left hands.

Boogie-Woogie

A left hand that walks: eight to the bar on the blues

Open the Boogie-woogie style in the Backing Track

What it is

Blues piano with a left hand that never stops: eight notes to the bar, swung, repeating one figure up and down the chord while the right hand plays riffs, tremolos and blue notes against it. It is almost always a 12-bar blues.

Boogie-woogie and stride are close relations: both are piano music for dancing at parties, both put a band into the left hand, and the same pianists often played both. Stride’s left hand leaps between bass and chord on the beats; boogie-woogie’s walks along the bass in eighth notes. The lesson Two Left Hands plays them side by side.

A little history

The style began in the lumber, turpentine and railroad camps of Texas and Louisiana in the first years of the 1900s, played on “barrelhouse” pianos in the camps’ bars, and travelled north with the migration. In Chicago in the 1920s it was the music of rent parties, as stride was in Harlem. Pinetop Smith’s Pine Top’s Boogie Woogie (1928) gave the style its name; Jimmy Yancey, Meade Lux Lewis and Albert Ammons played it in Chicago.

In December 1938 the producer John Hammond put Ammons, Lewis and Pete Johnson on stage at Carnegie Hall in the From Spirituals to Swing concert, and boogie-woogie became a national craze. Big bands arranged it (Count Basie’s Boogie Woogie, Tommy Dorsey’s version of Pinetop’s piece), and the Andrews Sisters sang it. Its eight-to-the-bar bass went into jump blues, rhythm and blues and early rock and roll: Chuck Berry’s guitar plays a boogie left hand.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Boogie-woogie: swung eighths walking up the chord and back down, root 3rd 5th 6th flat-7th 6th 5th 3rd, every bar. The pianist’s left hand, on the bass.
  • Comping: Boogie-woogie right hand: a two-bar riff of short swung chords against the bass.
  • Drums: Blues shuffle: swung eighths on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
  • Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Boogie-woogie pianists have dozens of left-hand patterns (rolling octaves, the Yancey bass, broken sixths) and their right hands play the lead. The band’s bassist has one pattern and its pianist one riff, so a melody or a solo on top is your part.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
Meade Lux Lewis, Honky Tonk Train Blues 1927 A train in the left hand, cross-rhythms in the right.
Pinetop Smith, Pine Top’s Boogie Woogie 1928 The record that named the style; Smith calls out to the dancers.
Albert Ammons, Boogie Woogie Stomp 1936 The walking left hand at full power.
Count Basie, Boogie Woogie (with Jimmy Rushing) 1936 Boogie-woogie from a small swing band.
Big Joe Turner and Pete Johnson, Roll ’Em Pete 1938 Boogie-woogie under a blues shouter: a short step to rock and roll.
Jimmy Yancey, Yancey Stomp 1939 A lighter, older Chicago style.
More recent
Recording Year Listen for
Jerry Lee Lewis, Whole Lotta Shakin’ Goin’ On 1957 The boogie left hand in rock and roll.

Sources

  • Peter J. Silvester, A Left Hand Like God: A History of Boogie-Woogie Piano (Quartet, 1988).
  • Ted Gioia, The History of Jazz (Oxford, 1997), on Chicago and the 1938 Carnegie Hall concert.
  • Riccardo Scivales, Jazz Piano: The Left Hand (Ekay, 1990), on stride and boogie-woogie left hands.

Jump Blues

Boogie-woogie for a small band, loud, on the backbeat

Open the Jump blues style in the Backing Track

What it is

Up-tempo blues for dancing, played by small bands of the 1940s: a rhythm section, two or three horns riffing together, and a singer. The bass plays the boogie-woogie left hand, the drums play a shuffle with a hard backbeat on 2 and 4, and the horns and piano play short riffs. It is the bridge from swing and boogie-woogie to rhythm and blues and rock and roll.

A little history

When the big bands became too costly during the Second World War, many of their players formed small groups that kept the swing bands’ riffs and the boogie-woogie bass but played them louder, on the backbeat, for dancers and jukeboxes. Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five were the most popular: Caldonia (1945) and Choo Choo Ch’Boogie (1946) topped the race-record charts, which Billboard renamed rhythm and blues in 1949. Big Joe Turner, Wynonie Harris, Roy Brown and Amos Milburn sang it; Lionel Hampton’s Flying Home gave it a honking tenor sax. By the early 1950s the same music, with an electric guitar in front, was being called rock and roll.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Boogie-woogie: swung eighths, root 3rd 5th 6th flat-7th 6th 5th 3rd.
  • Comping: Boogie-woogie right hand: a two-bar riff of short swung chords.
  • Drums: Jump blues: the shuffle on the cymbal, the kick feathered on every beat, a loud snare on 2 and 4.
  • Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

The horns are what most people remember of a jump band, and the band has none. Play the riffs yourself, or sing.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
Lionel Hampton, Flying Home 1942 Illinois Jacquet’s tenor solo, the model for every honking sax after it.
Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five, Caldonia 1945 Riffing horns over a shuffle; the singer as entertainer.
Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five, Choo Choo Ch’Boogie 1946 A boogie bass under a country-flavoured song.
Roy Brown, Good Rockin’ Tonight 1947 The backbeat that rock and roll took.
Big Joe Turner, Shake, Rattle and Roll 1954 Jump blues on the edge of rock and roll.

Sources

  • Arnold Shaw, Honkers and Shouters: The Golden Years of Rhythm and Blues (Collier, 1978).
  • John Chilton, Let the Good Times Roll: The Story of Louis Jordan and His Music (Michigan, 1994).

Latin

Bossa nova

Root-and-fifth bass, a two-bar comping pattern and the bossa clave

Open the Bossa nova style in the Backing Track

What it is

Brazilian song style from Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s: samba slowed and quietened for a voice and a nylon-string guitar. The guitarist’s thumb plays the bass on beats 1 and 3 (in 2/4 counting, the two beats of the bar) while the fingers play syncopated chords that repeat over two bars.

A little history

Samba’s percussion section (the surdo bass drum, tamborim, agogô) was too loud for the small apartments and clubs of Copacabana. João Gilberto moved the parts onto the guitar: the thumb took the surdo, the fingers took the tamborim’s syncopations. His single Chega de Saudade (1958, song by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes) is usually called the first bossa nova record. Jobim’s harmony (major sevenths, ninths, chromatic inner lines) came from jazz and from Debussy and Ravel.

American jazz musicians took it up after Charlie Byrd and Stan Getz’s Jazz Samba (1962). Getz/Gilberto (recorded 1963, released 1964), with Astrud Gilberto singing The Girl from Ipanema, made it a world style. Jazz drummers turned the guitar’s rhythm into the brush or cross-stick pattern the band plays: a two-bar figure close to the son clave, over a steady bass drum on 1 and 3.

The band’s version

  • Bass: root and fifth with pickups. Comping: the two-bar pattern.
  • Drums: bossa clave on the cross-stick. Voicings: jazz voicings with added 9ths.
  • Feel: straight eighths. Bossa never swings.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
João Gilberto, Chega de Saudade 1958 The guitar rhythm that started it.
Stan Getz & Charlie Byrd, Desafinado (Jazz Samba) 1962 The first American hit version.
Stan Getz & João Gilberto, The Girl from Ipanema 1964 Milton Banana’s drums; Jobim on piano.
Antônio Carlos Jobim, Wave 1967 Jobim’s own arrangement, Ron Carter on bass.
Elis Regina & Tom Jobim, Águas de Março 1974 A later, freer bossa groove.
More recent
Recording Year Listen for
Bebel Gilberto, Samba da Bênção (Tanto Tempo) 2000 João Gilberto’s daughter: bossa with electronic beats.
Laufey, From the Start 2023 A bossa groove that went viral: guitar rhythm, cross-stick, root-and-fifth bass.

Sources

  • Ruy Castro, Bossa Nova: The Story of the Brazilian Music That Seduced the World (A Cappella, 2000).
  • Chris McGowan and Ricardo Pessanha, The Brazilian Sound (Temple, 2009 ed.).

Son montuno

Tumbao bass, the montuno, son clave and congas

Open the Son montuno style in the Backing Track

What it is

The groove of Cuban son and of salsa: a two-bar repeating piano figure (the montuno or guajeo), a bass that plays ahead of the beat (the tumbao), and a clave pattern every part is fitted to.

A little history

Son grew up in eastern Cuba and reached Havana around 1910-20, played by small groups on tres (a guitar with three doubled strings), guitar, bongó, maracas, claves and a marímbula or bass. The second half of a son, the montuno, is a vamp where a lead singer improvises against a chorus. In the late 1930s and 1940s Arsenio Rodríguez enlarged the group into the conjunto: piano, trumpets, and a conga. He is credited with the anticipated bass: the bass skips beat 1 and lands on the and of 2 and on 4, so that each chord is heard a little before the bar it belongs to. Mambo bands (Pérez Prado, Machito) and the New York salsa of the 1960s and ’70s (Eddie Palmieri, Fania Records) built on the same parts.

Clave is the two-bar rhythm (3-2: three hits then two; or 2-3) that the parts are written around. The band plays 2-3.

The band’s version

  • Bass: tumbao, anticipating each bar. Comping: the two-bar montuno.
  • Drums: clave. Congas: a tumbao moving to the second drum every other bar.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
Septeto Nacional (Ignacio Piñeiro), Échale salsita 1930 Early son with the old sextet line-up.
Arsenio Rodríguez y su Conjunto, Dame un cachito pa’ huelé 1946 The conjunto sound and the anticipated bass.
Machito and his Afro-Cubans, Tanga composed 1943, recorded later in the 1940s Son and mambo meeting big-band jazz.
Eddie Palmieri, Azúcar Pa’ Ti 1965 The piano montuno stretched out over a long vamp.
Buena Vista Social Club, Chan Chan 1997 Compay Segundo’s son; easy to count the clave.
More recent
Recording Year Listen for

Cha-cha

A steady bell and the cha-cha-chá on 3, the and of 3, and 4

Open the Cha-cha style in the Backing Track

What it is

A medium-tempo Cuban dance rhythm, steadier and simpler than mambo, with a cowbell on every beat and the three quick steps (cha-cha-chá) on beat 3, the and of 3, and beat 4.

A little history

Violinist Enrique Jorrín, of the charanga orchestra Orquesta América, wrote La engañadora (1951, recorded 1953). The orchestra’s dancers found its rhythm easier than the danzón-mambo, and the steps’ scuffing sound named the dance. Charangas played it on flute, violins, piano, bass, timbales, güiro and conga; Orquesta Aragón made it famous across Latin America. By the late 1950s it was a ballroom dance in the US and Europe, and American pop recorded “cha-cha” versions of everything.

The band’s version

  • Bass: the cha-cha bass line. Comping: chords on the cha-cha figure.
  • Drums: a bell on the beats. Congas: a tumbao. Voicings: plain triads and sevenths.

Tango

The habanera rhythm in the bass and chords

Open the Tango style in the Backing Track

What it is

The dance music of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, in 2/4 or 4/4, played here on its oldest rhythm: the habanera (dotted eighth, sixteenth, two eighths), which also underlies the 3+3+2 of a lot of later pop.

A little history

The habanera was a Cuban song and dance of the mid-1800s that spread through Spain, Mexico and the Río de la Plata ports (Bizet borrowed one for Carmen, 1875). In the poor neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires in the 1880s and ’90s it mixed with the milonga, Spanish and Italian song, and African Argentine candombe into the tango. Early groups were flute, violin and guitar; the bandoneón (a German button accordion) arrived around 1900 and became the tango’s voice. Carlos Gardel’s Mi noche triste (1917) began the sung tango. The 1940s orquestas típicas (Juan D’Arienzo, Aníbal Troilo, Osvaldo Pugliese) moved to a driving marcato in four; from the 1950s Astor Piazzolla’s nuevo tango added jazz and classical counterpoint.

The band plays the habanera rhythm, the older and more widely useful of tango’s rhythms; the four-beat marcato of the dance orchestras is not modelled.

Caribbean

Calypso

Root-and-fifth bass with chords on every off-beat

Open the Calypso style in the Backing Track

What it is

The topical song of Trinidad: a singer (the calypsonian) with a witty, often political lyric over a bouncing 2/4, with a strummed guitar or cuatro, a bass on root and fifth, and chords on the off-beats.

A little history

Calypso (earlier kaiso) grew out of the songs of Trinidad’s Carnival in the 1800s: the chantwell leading call-and-response songs in French Creole, stick-fighting songs, and the music of the Spanish Venezuelan string bands. By the 1910s-20s it was sung in English and recorded in New York. Calypso tents competed each Carnival season, and singers took grand names: Atilla the Hun, Roaring Lion, Lord Invader, Lord Kitchener, the Mighty Sparrow. Lord Invader’s Rum and Coca-Cola (sung at the 1943 Carnival) became an American hit for the Andrews Sisters in 1945, and Invader later won a lawsuit over its royalties; and Harry Belafonte’s album Calypso (1956) was the first LP to sell a million copies. Jamaica’s mento is a cousin, and in the 1970s Lord Shorty mixed calypso with Indian rhythms into soca, now Carnival’s main music.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: chords on every off-beat. Drums: a calypso beat.

Ska / reggae

Off-beat chords over a one-drop

Open the Ska / reggae style in the Backing Track

What it is

Jamaican popular music since about 1960: guitar and keyboard chords on the off-beats (the skank), a bass that carries the melody of the groove, and, in reggae, a one-drop drum beat with nothing on beat 1 and the kick and snare (or rim) together on beat 3.

A little history

Ska (c. 1960-66) came from Jamaican musicians playing American R&B for sound systems and stressing the off-beat; studio bands such as the Skatalites played it fast with horns. Around 1966 the tempo slowed into rocksteady, with the bass more prominent (Alton Ellis, the Paragons). By 1968 the beat had changed again into reggae: Toots and the Maytals’ Do the Reggay (1968) is one of the first records to use the word. Drummer Carlton Barrett of Bob Marley’s Wailers made the one-drop the standard reggae beat, and Island Records’ Catch a Fire (1973) took the Wailers worldwide. Later strands include dub, roots, lovers rock, dancehall (see Reggaeton) and Britain’s 2 Tone ska revival (c. 1979).

The band’s version

  • Bass: Roots on every beat, plainer than a real reggae bass line, which moves and leaves gaps.
  • Comping: off-beat chords. Drums: one-drop.

Reggaeton

The dembow drum pattern under long chords, the bass on a 3+3+2

Open the Reggaeton style in the Backing Track

What it is

Spanish-language dance music from Puerto Rico and Panama, built on the dembow: the kick on every beat, and the snare on the last sixteenth of beat 1 and the and of 2 (and again in beats 3 and 4), a 3+3+2 in sixteenths over each half bar, under long synth chords and a rapped or sung vocal.

A little history

The rhythm is named after Shabba Ranks’ Jamaican dancehall record Dem Bow (1990), whose riddim (the backing track, by Steely & Clevie, built on their Poco Man Jam) was copied everywhere. In Panama, artists such as El General sang Spanish lyrics over dancehall riddims (reggae en español). In Puerto Rico in the 1990s DJ Playero and others made underground mixtapes on the same beats; the name reggaeton took hold around the turn of the century. Daddy Yankee’s Gasolina (2004) was the international breakthrough, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee’s Despacito (2017) one of the most-streamed songs ever, and Bad Bunny the genre’s biggest star of the 2020s.

The band’s version

  • Bass: 3+3+2 (tresillo). Comping: long held chords. Drums: dembow.

Folk, rock and pop

Straight-eighth rock

Root eighths, down-up strumming and a backbeat

Open the Straight-eighth rock style in the Backing Track

What it is

The basic rock band: drums with a snare backbeat on 2 and 4 and even eighth notes on the hi-hat, an electric bass on the root in eighths, and guitar strumming every eighth note.

A little history

Rhythm and blues of the late 1940s and early ’50s was mostly shuffled (swung) eighths. Through the 1950s, records by Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Ray Charles mixed straight eighths in, and by the early 1960s even eighths were the norm in rock and soul; Alexander Stewart traces the shift through New Orleans drummers such as Earl Palmer. The backbeat came from gospel handclaps and R&B. The British Invasion, then punk’s down-stroke eighths (the Ramones, 1976) and new wave, kept the plain driving eighths at the centre of the style.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Root eighths. Comping: down-up eighths on the guitar. Drums: a backbeat whose kick varies from bar to bar. Chords are pushed (they arrive an eighth early) the way rock bands do.

Emo / pop-punk

Palm-muted power chords that open up in the chorus

Open the Emo / pop-punk style in the Backing Track

What it is

Guitar-band rock at punk tempos with melodic, often confessional singing: a distorted guitar chugging palm-muted power chords in the verse, ringing open in the chorus, over root eighths and a rock beat, with half-time choruses and breakdowns.

A little history

Emo (“emotional hardcore”) began in Washington, D.C., in 1985 with Rites of Spring and Embrace, who took hardcore punk’s speed into more personal songs. The 1990s brought a quieter, intricate “Midwest emo” (Cap’n Jazz, American Football). Pop-punk runs from the Buzzcocks and the Ramones to Green Day’s Dookie (1994), which sold millions, then Blink-182. Around 2000-2007 the two merged into a mainstream sound: Jimmy Eat World, My Chemical Romance, Fall Out Boy, Paramore. It came back in the 2020s, from Olivia Rodrigo to a revival of the bands themselves.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Root eighths. Comping: palm-muted chugging in verses, open strumming in Chorus bars.
  • Drums: rock backbeat; mark bars Half-time for a half-time chorus or breakdown.

Acoustic strum

A steel-string guitar over a light backbeat

Open the Acoustic strum style in the Backing Track

What it is

The singer-songwriter’s band: a steel-string acoustic guitar strumming a syncopated pattern (down, down-up, up-down-up), a bass and kick together on 1, the and of 2, and 3, and a light backbeat.

A little history

The steel-string guitar became a popular accompanying instrument through country and blues players in the 1920s-30s and the folk revival of the 1950s-60s (Woody Guthrie, then Bob Dylan, Joan Baez). From the late 1960s singer-songwriters (James Taylor, Joni Mitchell, Cat Stevens) put a band around the strummed guitar. The 1990s Britpop and “unplugged” years (Oasis’s Wonderwall) and the 2000s-2010s folk-pop of Jason Mraz, Mumford & Sons and Ed Sheeran kept it among the most common sounds in pop.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Dotted (1, and of 2, 3), with the kick. Comping: a campfire strum. Drums: light.

Piano ballad

Left-hand octaves, a broken right hand, half-time drums

Open the Piano ballad style in the Backing Track

What it is

The slow pop or rock song led from the piano: octaves in the left hand, the chord broken or rocked in the right (often in first inversion, so the top moves smoothly), and a band that comes in half-time, with the backbeat on beat 3.

A little history

The piano was the home instrument of popular song long before rock: Tin Pan Alley sold sheet music for it. In the 1970s singer-songwriters at the piano (Carole King’s Tapestry, 1971; Elton John; Billy Joel) made the piano ballad a staple of rock. The 1980s power ballad put it under big drums, and from the 2000s Coldplay, Alicia Keys and Adele (Someone Like You, 2011, over nothing but broken piano chords) kept it at the top of the charts.

The band’s version

  • Comping: three right-hand patterns (rocking, half-broken, syncopated) in four-bar spans.
  • Bass and drums: half time; a quiet kick and a cross-stick on 3. The hi-hat sits low.

Dance pop

Four on the floor, open hi-hat off-beats, octave bass

Open the Dance pop style in the Backing Track

What it is

The disco beat and its descendants: a kick drum on every beat (four on the floor), the open hi-hat on every off-beat, a bass jumping between the root and its octave, and chords on a 3+3+2.

A little history

Disco grew out of New York and Philadelphia clubs in the early 1970s. Earl Young, the drummer of Philadelphia International’s house band MFSB, is often credited with the steady kick and open hi-hat (The Love I Lost, Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes, 1973). The octave bass became disco’s other mark (Chic’s Bernard Edwards). Giorgio Moroder and Donna Summer’s I Feel Love (1977) put the beat on synthesizers and pointed toward house and techno (Chicago and Detroit, mid-1980s). Since then the four-on-the-floor beat has stayed at the centre of dance pop: Madonna, Kylie Minogue, Daft Punk, Dua Lipa.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Octaves. Comping: a 3+3+2, on the electric piano. Drums: four on the floor.

Motown / soul

Snare on every beat, tambourine on 2 and 4

Open the Motown / soul style in the Backing Track

What it is

The 1960s Detroit sound of Motown Records: a snare (often with a tambourine) hitting every beat, a busy electric bass, guitars chopping chords, and a song built for radio and dancing.

A little history

Berry Gordy started Motown in Detroit in 1959. Its records were cut by a house band later known as the Funk Brothers: drummer Benny Benjamin, bassist James Jamerson, pianist Earl Van Dyke, and others, playing in Studio A (“the Snakepit”). The songwriting team Holland-Dozier-Holland wrote the mid-’60s run of hits for the Supremes and the Four Tops, many on a stomping four-beat snare. Jamerson’s bass lines, played with one finger on a Fender Precision, moved far more than any pattern can show. The band played uncredited until the film Standing in the Shadows of Motown (2002).

The band’s version

  • Bass: Motown: root, fifth, octave, a stand-in for Jamerson’s lines.
  • Comping: the two-bar rhythm of You Can’t Hurry Love. Drums: snare on every beat.

12/8 doo-wop

Triplet piano chords over a slow backbeat

Open the 12/8 doo-wop style in the Backing Track

What it is

The slow 1950s ballad: piano chords repeated in triplets, three to every beat, over a slow backbeat, usually on the I-vi-IV-V chords, behind a lead singer and vocal group.

A little history

Doo-wop came from African American vocal groups on street corners in New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Chicago in the late 1940s and ’50s, following the Ink Spots and the Mills Brothers. The backing singers sang nonsense syllables (doo-wop, sh-boom) in place of instruments. On record, small bands added a pianist hammering triplets, an idea from New Orleans rhythm and blues (Fats Domino) and the slow blues. The same 12/8 feel carries soul ballads into the 1960s, from Etta James’s At Last onward.

The band’s version

  • Bass: 12/8 ballad. Comping: triplets. Drums: slow 12/8 backbeat.
  • On a 4/4 chart the band plays the triplets over each beat.

Country train beat

Boom-chicka strum and the snare on every eighth

Open the Country train beat style in the Backing Track

What it is

The country rhythm that sounds like a steam train: a snare (often with brushes) on every eighth note, accented on 2 and 4, a bass on root and fifth, and a boom-chicka guitar.

A little history

The sound is most associated with Johnny Cash’s Tennessee Two at Sun Records in Memphis: Luther Perkins’ muted boom-chicka electric guitar and Marshall Grant’s slapped bass on Folsom Prison Blues (1955) and I Walk the Line (1956). Drummer W. S. Holland joined in 1960 and the train beat became a drum pattern. Train songs had been part of country and blues since the 1920s (Jimmie Rodgers), and the beat has stayed in rockabilly, bluegrass-flavoured country and country rock.

  • Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: a boom-chicka strum. Drums: train beat.

Boom-chick

Bass on 1 and 3, chords on 2 and 4; oom-pah-pah in 3/4

Open the Boom-chick style in the Backing Track

What it is

The oldest accompaniment in popular music: a bass note on the strong beats and a chord on the weak ones. In 2/4 or 4/4 it is boom-chick; in 3/4 it is oom-pah-pah.

A little history

Brass bands and dance orchestras of the 1800s split the beat between the tuba (or bass) and the horns or second violins: marches, polkas and waltzes all run on it, and so does the stride and ragtime piano left hand (bass note, chord, bass note, chord). Guitarists in American old-time and country music used the same idea, a thumbed bass on the beat and a strum after it: Maybelle Carter’s guitar with the Carter Family from 1927, and later the folk revival. Sing-along songs from campfire to music hall still use it.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: oompah. Drums: boom-chick.

Freylekhs / polka

Bass on every beat, the whole chord on every off-beat

Open the Freylekhs / polka style in the Backing Track

What it is

The fast 2/4 of Eastern European dance music: the bass on every beat, alternating root and fifth, and the full chord on every off-beat (oom-pa oom-pa). A freylekhs (“joyful”) is the most common klezmer dance tune; the polka is its Central European cousin.

A little history

The polka started in Bohemia in the 1830s and was danced across Europe and America within a decade. Its bands (brass, then accordion) gave it the bass-and-off-beat accompaniment. Klezmer is the instrumental music of Ashkenazi Jewish weddings in Eastern Europe. Immigrant clarinettists Naftule Brandwein and Dave Tarras recorded it in New York in the 1920s, with bands that played the same driving off-beats on piano, brass and drums. It faded after the war and came back in the 1970s revival (the Klezmorim, Andy Statman, Kapelye, later the Klezmatics). Songs like Hava Nagila and Hanukkah songs are still played this way.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Root and fifth on every beat, with a run up into the next bar now and then.
  • Comping: chords on the off-beats. In half-time bars the piano switches to ballad patterns.

Listening

John Prine Fingerpicking

Thumb on alternating bass strings, fingers pinching on 2 and 4

Open the John Prine Fingerpicking style in the Backing Track

What it is

A steel-string guitar played with the thumb and fingers at once: the thumb alternates between two bass strings on every beat while the fingers pluck the chord on the off-beats or pinch with the thumb. No drums, an upright bass doubling the thumb.

A little history

Alternating-thumb picking runs back to Black guitarists in the South of the 1920s: Mississippi John Hurt recorded for OKeh in 1928, and Elizabeth Cotten played Freight Train left-handed. In Kentucky, Arnold Shultz, Ike Everly and Mose Rager handed it to Merle Travis, after whom “Travis picking” is named, and Chet Atkins spread it through country guitar. The 1960s folk revival brought it to singer-songwriters. John Prine (1946-2020), the Chicago postman whose first album (John Prine, 1971) contains Paradise, Hello in There and Angel from Montgomery, played a plain thumb-and-fingers style under plain-spoken songs.

The band’s version

  • Comping: the prine and travis patterns. Bass: root and fifth with the thumb. Drums: none.

Hymns and carols

Waltz (in one)

A quick 3/4 felt one to the bar

Open the Waltz (in one) style in the Backing Track

What it is

A fast 3/4 in which the listener feels one beat a bar, not three: the bass on 1, light chords on 2 and 3, brushes, bars grouped in fours.

A little history

The waltz rose from Austrian and South German country dances in the late 1700s and took over the ballrooms of Vienna in the early 1800s with Joseph Lanner and the Strauss family (Johann Strauss II’s The Blue Danube, 1867). Played fast, the pulse is one per bar, and phrases come in fours and eights. The waltz then spread everywhere: music-hall and parlour songs, country waltzes (Tennessee Waltz), jazz waltzes, and many carols and folk songs that are sung in a quick 3/4.

The band’s version

  • Bass: root on 1 (root one bar, fifth the next). Comping: waltz. Drums: brushed waltz.

Listening

Hymn (four parts)

Every chord held until the next, the bass doubling the root

Open the Hymn (four parts) style in the Backing Track

What it is

Congregational hymn accompaniment: soprano, alto, tenor and bass moving together, one chord per melody note or two, each held until the next, no drums. The organ is the obvious instrument.

A little history

Martin Luther’s chorales (from the 1520s) gave Protestant congregations hymns to sing; J. S. Bach’s four-part harmonisations of them in his cantatas and passions (1720s-40s) became the model of how to write harmony, and still are in theory classes. In England, Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley in the 1700s wrote the texts; the collection Hymns Ancient and Modern (1861) and The English Hymnal (1906, music edited by Ralph Vaughan Williams) set the four-part style of the Anglican hymnal. American hymnals, gospel song and shape-note singing grew from the same roots.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Held roots. Comping: hymn: three voices over the root. Drums: none.
  • Choose Church organ as the instrument for the other obvious sound.

Listening

Folk carol

Strummed guitar, bass on 1 and 3, very light time

Open the Folk carol style in the Backing Track

What it is

Traditional carols played by a folk-rock band: a strummed steel-string guitar, upright bass on 1 and 3, light brushes. Between the four-part hymn and acoustic strum.

A little history

Many English carols are older than the hymns sung beside them: dance songs and wassails collected by Cecil Sharp and Ralph Vaughan Williams in the early 1900s and published in The Oxford Book of Carols (1928). The British folk revival of the 1960s and the folk-rock bands that followed (Steeleye Span, Fairport Convention) played them with guitars, fiddles and drums, and many carol albums since have done the same.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Roots on 1 and 3. Comping: folk strum. Drums: brushes, very light.
